title: The Accusative
summary: The case of the direct object: den and einen and keinen in the masculine singular, the nouns that take -en with them, the accusative of every personal pronoun, wen against wer, uns and euch and sich for one another, the pronouns that take no ending against welch- which does, and the three verbs that take no accusative at all.

rules.heading: The accusative marks the direct object
rules.statement: German marks the part a noun plays in its sentence by case. The accusative is the case of the direct object — the person or thing the action of the verb lands on.

examples.gloss: The man is reading the book.
We are looking for the woman.

footnotes: The inventory's name for this element of the sentence is the *Akkusativergänzung*.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §2.2.1, p. 35, on the accusative as the case of the direct object; §18.3.1, p. 361, on the Akkusativergänzung.

rules.heading: The definite article in the accusative
rules.statement: **der** becomes **den** in the accusative. The feminine **die**, the neuter **das** and the plural **die** are the same in both cases, so the masculine singular is the only place the accusative and the nominative differ.

examples.gloss: The man is buying the chair.
The man is buying the cat.
The man is buying the car.
The man is buying the books.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §2.2.1, p. 35, with Table 1.5, p. 26, for the declension of the article.

rules.heading: ein and kein in the accusative
rules.statement: **ein** becomes **einen** and **kein** becomes **keinen** before a masculine singular. The feminine, neuter and plural forms are the same as in the nominative.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §2.2.1, p. 35, with Table 4.2, p. 64, for the ein-forms.

rules.heading: The masculine nouns that take -en
rules.statement: A group of masculine nouns adds **-n** or **-en** in every case but the nominative singular. In these the accusative changes the noun as well as its article.

examples.gloss: She is looking for the boy.

footnotes: *der Herr* takes **-n** in the singular and **-en** in the plural: *den Herrn*, *die Herren*.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §1.3.2, on the weak masculine declension.

rules.heading: The personal pronouns in the accusative
rules.statement: Every personal pronoun has an accusative form of its own, so here the change is not confined to the masculine.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §3.1.1, p. 48, with Table 3.1, for the personal pronouns.

rules.heading: wen
rules.statement: **wen** asks after a person in the accusative, where **wer** asks after a person in the nominative (¶71). **was** is the same word in both cases.

examples.note: *wer* is the subject: it does the seeing.
*wen* is the object: it is seen.

rules.heading: uns, euch and sich as reciprocal pronouns
rules.statement: **uns**, **euch** and **sich** also stand where two or more people do something to one another. **sich** serves the third person in both numbers and the polite **Sie**.

examples.gloss: We are seeing each other tomorrow.
They are meeting each other here.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §3.2.7, p. 51, on the reflexive and reciprocal pronouns.

rules.heading: etwas, nichts, alles and mehr
rules.statement: **etwas**, **nichts**, **alles** and **mehr** take no ending. Each stands in the accusative in the form it has in the nominative.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §5.5.1 on alles, §5.5.9 on etwas, §5.5.22 on nichts.

rules.heading: welch-
rules.statement: **welch-** declines like the definite article, and so takes **-en** before a masculine singular in the accusative.

examples.gloss: Which cat are you looking for?

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.

rules.heading: sein, werden and bleiben take no accusative
rules.statement: **sein**, **werden** and **bleiben** are followed by a complement in the nominative rather than by an accusative object (¶67). A profession after **sein** stands with no article at all (¶45).

examples.gloss: The child is becoming a man.

examples.note: No article at all with the profession.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §2.1.3, p. 33, and §18.1.3, p. 356, on the nominative complement.

rules.heading: Prepositions that fix the accusative
rules.statement: A preposition fixes the case of the noun that follows it. **für** and **ohne** fix the accusative.

examples.target: Das Buch ist für den Mann.
examples.gloss: The book is for the man.
He is coming without the car.

footnotes: *durch*, *gegen*, *um*, *entlang*, *wider* and *bis* govern the accusative as well, and are taken up with the prepositions.
Nine further prepositions govern the accusative for a movement towards something and the dative for a position at it.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §20, on the prepositions and the cases they govern.

rules.heading: A measure stands in the accusative
rules.statement: A price, a weight, a distance or a height stands in the accusative, with no preposition in front of it.
footnotes: This is why *Was kostet die Fahrkarte?* has *was* in the accusative: the price is a measure, and *die Fahrkarte* is the subject the verb agrees with.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.

vocabulary.notes: A weak masculine: **-en** in every case but the nominative singular (¶80).
A weak masculine with **-n** in the singular and **-en** in the plural (¶80).
After a numeral the plural is *die Euro*: *drei Euro*.
The stem vowel changes in the second and third person singular (¶61).
The stem vowel changes in the second and third person singular (¶61).
The stem vowel changes in the second and third person singular (¶61).
*es gibt* — *there is, there are* — takes an accusative object and does not change for number: *Es gibt hier einen Bahnhof*, *Es gibt keine Äpfel*.
Declines like the definite article: accusative *welchen, welche, welches* (¶85).

drills.explanation: *Apfel* is masculine and the object of *kaufen*, so *ein* becomes *einen* (¶79).
*Buch* is neuter, and the neuter article is the same in the accusative as in the nominative (¶78).

drills.stem: In which of these is the accusative form identical with the nominative?
drills.explanation: Feminine, neuter and plural do not change; the masculine singular does, giving *den Mann* (¶78).
*Stuhl* is masculine (¶32), and the masculine singular is the one place the accusative differs: *der* becomes *den* (¶78).
*er* becomes *ihn* in the accusative (¶81). *ihm* is the dative and *er* the nominative.

drills.stem: Pair each nominative pronoun with its accusative form.
drills.explanation: *ich → mich*, *du → dich*, *er → ihn*, *wir → uns* (¶81). *euch* is the accusative of *ihr*, which is not in Column I.

drills.stem: *____ siehst du?* — asking after a person as the object
drills.explanation: The person asked after is the object of *sehen*, so the accusative **wen** is the form (¶82). **wer** would make the person the one doing the seeing.

drills.stem: Which of these asks who is *being seen*?
drills.explanation: *Wen* is the accusative, so it is the one seen and *der Mann* the one seeing (¶82). The second question reverses the roles; the third and fourth put two nominatives or two accusatives in one sentence, leaving it without a subject or without an object.
**sich** serves the third person only; the first person plural takes **uns** and the second **euch** (¶83).
**welch-** declines like the definite article, and *Apfel* is a masculine singular object, so the ending is **-en** (¶85), matching the *den* of ¶78.

drills.stem: Which of these take no ending in the accusative?
drills.explanation: *etwas*, *nichts*, *alles* and *mehr* are indeclinable (¶84). *welch-* is the one of the group that declines (¶85).

drills.stem: *Sie fragt uns.* Which person does *uns* stand for?
drills.explanation: *uns* is the accusative of *wir*, the first person plural (¶81). *Sie* is third person and is the subject here.
*sein* takes a complement in the nominative, not an accusative object (¶86, ¶67), so *einen* is wrong here however masculine *Apfel* is.

drills.stem: *Er ist Lehrer.* Which of these hold?
options: *Lehrer* stands with no article because it is a profession after *sein*
*Lehrer* is a complement in the nominative
drills.explanation: A profession after *sein* takes no article (¶45), and what follows *sein* is a nominative complement (¶86), so *ist* has no object at all — which is what rules out the fourth.
*der Student* is a weak masculine and takes **-en** in every case but the nominative singular (¶80), so the accusative is *den Studenten*.

drills.stem: *Wir fragen den Menschen.* Which numbered rule accounts for the **-en** on the noun?
drills.explanation: ¶80: *der Mensch* is a weak masculine and adds **-en** outside the nominative singular. ¶78 accounts for the *den* in front of it, but not for the ending on the noun.

A yes/no question puts the finite verb first (¶75); *essen* changes its stem vowel in the second person singular (¶61), and the stem already ends in a double s, so the ending adds no further one (¶58).
**für** fixes the accusative (¶87), and the masculine singular accusative article is *den* (¶78).

drills.stem: Pair each phrase with what accounts for the form it has.
columnII: a masculine singular direct object, so *ein* becomes *einen*
a complement after *sein*, so the nominative stands
a profession after *sein*, so no article at all
a weak masculine, so the noun itself takes **-en**
a feminine object, so the article does not change
drills.explanation: *einen Apfel* is ¶79, *ein Apfel* after *ist* is ¶86, the bare *Lehrer* is ¶45, and *den Studenten* is ¶80. The last label describes a feminine object and fits none of the four.
A price is a measure and stands in the accusative (¶88); *Euro* is masculine, so the form is *einen*. The subject of *kostet* is *das Buch*, which is why the verb is third person singular.

drills.title: Anna und der Bäcker
drills.passage:
ANNA. Guten Tag! Ich brauche Brot.
BÄCKER. Wir haben Brot und Kuchen. Was nehmen Sie?
ANNA. Ich nehme das Brot. Und einen Kuchen.
BÄCKER. Wie viele Kuchen brauchen Sie?
ANNA. Zwei. Was kostet das Brot?
BÄCKER. Das Brot kostet einen Euro. Die Kuchen kosten drei Euro.
ANNA. Gut. Haben Sie auch Äpfel?
BÄCKER. Nein, wir haben keine Äpfel. Es gibt hier einen Markt.
drills.translation: ANNA. Good day! I need bread. — BAKER. We have bread and cake. What are you taking? — ANNA. I'll take the bread. And a cake. — BAKER. How many cakes do you need? — ANNA. Two. What does the bread cost? — BAKER. The bread costs one euro. The cakes cost three euros. — ANNA. Good. Do you have apples too? — BAKER. No, we have no apples. There is a market here.

questions.explanation: *Ich nehme das Brot. Und einen Kuchen.* The market is what the baker mentions at the end, and there are no apples at all.
*Wie viele Kuchen brauchen Sie? — Zwei.* The three in the dialogue is the price of the cakes, not their number.
*Das Brot kostet einen Euro.* Three euros is what the cakes cost.

questions.stem: *Wir haben keine Äpfel.* Which of these hold?
options: *keine* is the accusative plural, identical with the nominative plural
*Äpfel* is the plural of *der Apfel*, formed with the Umlaut alone
*haben* takes a complement in the nominative
questions.explanation: *kein* does not change in the plural accusative (¶79), *Äpfel* is the Umlaut-only plural of ¶35, and it is the object of *haben* (¶77). *haben* is not one of the three verbs that take a nominative complement (¶86).

sources.citation: Composed for this course.
sources.note: A dialogue in a baker's shop, built from the accusative of ¶77–¶88, the present tense of ¶51–¶68 and the questions of ¶69–¶76. It leans on §2.2.1 of Hammer for the accusative object and on the Goethe Wortliste for its vocabulary.
